data.title: Chip suppliers shrug off Huang’s exit
data.description:
POLICY RISKS: Executives cited Nvidia’s CUDA software platform and lengthy supplier approvals as buffers, but said US export rules for China remained a concern

The departure of Nvidia Corp cofounder Jensen Huang (黃仁勳) could accelerate diversification in the artificial intelligence (AI) chip market but is unlikely to significantly disrupt Taiwan’s semiconductor supply chain, industry executives and investment advisers said yesterday.

Nvidia announced on Thursday that Huang had resigned as its president, CEO and a member of its board. The company did not give a reason for his departure.

Nvidia appointed chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent successor.

Huang’s resignation could accelerate the diversification of AI chip orders, potentially benefiting Nvidia rivals AMD and Broadcom, as well as Amazon and Google, which are developing their own application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs), or chips designed for specific tasks, Taishin Securities Investment Advisory (台新投顧) said in a report released yesterday.

Several senior semiconductor industry executives interviewed by CNA said ASIC development could gain momentum, but they did not expect it to significantly alter the competitive balance between ASICs and graphics processing units (GPUs), key to Nvidia’s AI business. Nvidia’s GPUs would be hard to replace because many AI developers rely on CUDA, Nvidia’s software platform for developing and running AI applications, which is designed to work with its chips, an executive in the semiconductor substrate industry said.

Despite a potential shift in AI chip demand from GPUs to ASICs, Taiwan’s chip suppliers are expected to face limited disruption because chipmakers maintain close relationships with Taiwanese suppliers, according to Taishin’s report.

Mega International Investment Services (兆豐國際投顧) vice president Alex Huang (黃國偉) also said Nvidia’s leadership change was unlikely to significantly affect Taiwanese suppliers, which remain integral to the AI supply chain amid rising demand and efforts to reduce reliance on China.

Individual suppliers will continue to adjust their operations in response to changes in product demand and technological developments, Alex Huang added.

An executive at a semiconductor packaging and testing company said the company might reallocate some of its 2027 budget to mitigate risks in the short term.

In the longer term, GPUs and ASICs had promising prospects, and the company would continue serving both markets based on customer demand, the executive said.

Another semiconductor executive said the change in Nvidia’s leadership would not affect its orders from Taiwanese suppliers, as increasingly complex GPU technology and lengthy supplier qualification processes make it difficult for Nvidia to switch suppliers.

For Taiwan’s semiconductor suppliers, changes in US export policy toward China remain an issue to watch, including any revisions to the rules governing Nvidia’s H200 shipments, Taishin Securities Investment Advisory said.

The US currently requires export licenses for Nvidia’s H200 AI chips shipped to approved Chinese customers, with each application subject to a security review.

data.title: ASE investing NT$100 billion in Kaohsiung
data.description:
SCALING UP: Two new facilities are expected to generate NT$80 billion in annual revenue and 5,000 jobs, while ASE agreed to buy more AI Nose systems

ASE Technology Holding Co (日月光投控), the world’s biggest chip packager and tester, yesterday said it is investing NT$100 billion (US$3.05 billion) in two new manufacturing facilities in Kaohsiung’s Lujhu District (路竹), scaling up capacity to meet surging demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing hardware.

Subsidiary Advanced Semiconductor Engineering Inc (ASE, 日月光) officially inaugurated the first phase of its Lujhu fab while breaking ground on the second phase.

The facilities in the Southern Taiwan Science Park are the group’s first expansion into Taiwan’s science park system.

The two factories are expected to generate NT$80 billion in annual revenue and create 5,000 new jobs once the factories reach full capacity, ASE Holding said in a statement.

The Lujhu facilities would be the group’s second manufacturing hub, complementing its primary production complex and headquarters in Kaohsiung’s Nanzih District (楠梓), it said.

“Rapid development in AI and high-performance-computing [HPC] devices continues to boost demand for advanced chips and, thus, for advanced packaging technology and capacity,” ASE Inc executive vice president Mike Hung (洪松井) said in the statement.

“With advanced packaging emerging as a critical driver of semiconductor computing performance, ASE is proactively expanding its capacity, technological capabilities and talent pool,” Hung said.

ASE Holding last month raised its annual capital expenditure budget for the third time to US$11.5 billion, driven by expectations that customer demand next year would continue to outpace capacity, particularly for its leading-edge advanced packaging technologies used in AI chips.

The first-phase fab was converted from an idle flat-panel plant that the company acquired from AUO Corp (友達) in July for about NT$6.5 billion.

The investment in new capacity reflected the company’s long-term commitment to meeting global customer demand and deepening Taiwan’s competitive advantage in the global semiconductor supply chain, S.F. Wang (王頌斐), executive vice president of ASE Inc’s Kaohsiung unit, said in the statement.

ASE’s advanced packaging expansion in the Southern Taiwan Science Park would further strengthen Taiwan’s semiconductor supply chain — from wafer manufacturing to packaging and testing services to downstream companies — Science Park Bureau Director-General Alice Cheng (鄭秀絨) said in a statement.

The investment would also inject fresh growth momentum into southern Taiwan’s semiconductor hub, she added.

Separately, ASE Holding yesterday inked a US$9 million agreement with Ainos Inc to purchase 5,000 additional AI Nose systems, which digitize scent and chemical signals into machine-readable smell identification data, the Houston-based firm said in a statement.

The agreement represents the largest single purchase order by value in Ainos’ history and marks a new phase of commercial scale for its chemical intelligence platform in advanced semiconductor manufacturing, the statement said. The purchase follows the delivery of 1,400 systems under the companies’ previous US$2.1 million agreement.

data.title: Lutnick faces chip export scrutiny
data.description:
Fallout from Jensen Huang’s (黃仁勳) ouster as Nvidia Corp chief executive officer is reaching deep into Washington, where US Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick has drawn scrutiny over whether his department did enough to keep the company’s prized artificial intelligence chips out of China’s hands.

As the ultimate overseer of US export control programs, Lutnick would be accountable for any policy or enforcement gaps that allowed Nvidia’s AI processors to reach unauthorized Chinese buyers. For now, the Commerce chief has the blessing of President Donald Trump, who gave Lutnick a vote of confidence hours after Nvidia announced Huang’s resignation on Thursday.

Huang’s abrupt departure was prompted by revelations of an affair with a woman suspected by US officials of spying for China and whose Singapore-based company Megaspeed had been under investigation by Commerce for possible export control violations. Megaspeed has denied any wrongdoing, while the former Nvidia chief’s alleged romantic partner, Alice Huang (黃樂), is now in China.

In the aftermath, Congress is demanding answers from Lutnick and other Trump administration officials about decisions that might have made it easier for China to obtain Nvidia’s advanced semiconductors as well as the degree to which Silicon Valley leaders like Jensen Huang might have influenced policy.

Pressure on the administration and the tech sector is escalating a week after an election in which voters expressed intense frustrations over the impact of the AI boom.

“I would like for Secretary Lutnick ASAP to come testify before the Senate Banking Committee because we have a lot of bipartisan questions and concerns about what’s happened over the last year,” US Senator Jim Banks, an Indiana Republican, said in an interview on Fox News.

Late on Thursday night, US Commerce Department spokesperson Kristen Eichamer said in a statement that “Secretary Lutnick has proactively agreed to appear voluntarily before the Banking Committee to address their questions.”

Axios reported on Wednesday that Trump had authorized a new crackdown on companies suspected of diverting advanced AI chips to China, but that Lutnick delayed acting on the directive. US Representative Raja Krishnamoorthi, an Illinois Democrat, called the report “deeply, deeply disturbing.”

On at least three occasions earlier this year — in May, August and earlier this month — Trump approved taking action against suspected diversions of Nvidia chips to China, Axios reported.

This week’s events are “a freaking disaster at this point, and it deserves tremendous scrutiny not only by obviously Nvidia’s board, but by the intelligence community and the US government as well,” Krishnamoorthi said in an interview on Bloomberg Television on Wednesday.

Further complicating the dynamic are allegations by Democratic lawmakers that Lutnick’s sons, who hold leadership positions at Cantor Fitzgerald, are profiting off of policy decisions that he makes. Lutnick, who previously was CEO of Cantor, divested his stake as legally required before becoming secretary, and elevated his sons to top jobs at the firm.

People with ties to the White House, who asked not to be identified describing private conversations, said Lutnick has been marginalized within the administration for a while. At the same time, his exit has been predicted before but it has not happened.

data.title: Rugged computer demand to lift Getac sales next year
data.description:
Getac Holdings Corp (神基控股) yesterday said it expects revenue next year to grow 5 percent to 10 percent year-on-year, supported by robust growth in its rugged PC business, despite weak PC demand weighing on its consumer electronics mechanical components business.

Getac’s revenue in the first three quarters increased 10.7 percent year-on-year to NT$32.25 billion (US$982.09 million). The company makes rugged computers and supplies mechanical components for consumer electronics, vehicles and aerospace applications.

Last quarter, electronic products — mainly rugged notebooks and tablets — were Getac’s largest revenue contributor at 47 percent, followed by mechanical products at 39 percent and aerospace fasteners at 13 percent, Getac chairman and CEO James Hwang (黃明漢) told an earnings conference in Taipei.

Mechanical products include composite mechanical components, mainly parts for notebook computers and other consumer electronics, as well as automotive components, Hwang said.

Growth next year is expected to be supported by continued defense demand and new business development, he said.

The company has secured two new orders from US and European customers for rugged-computer-based ground control solutions for unmanned vehicles, which are expected to lift the business’s share of total revenue to between 5 percent and 10 percent next year, he said.

Revenue from composite mechanical components is expected to decline this year by slightly more than the previously estimated 8 percent to 12 percent due to weak notebook and consumer electronics demand, he said. The weakness is expected to extend into the first quarter of next year, he said.

Revenue from automotive mechanical components, by contrast, is expected to grow by slightly more than the original target of 5 percent to 10 percent, Hwang added.

To reflect surging costs of key components such as solid-state drives, Getac raised rugged computer retail prices in the first quarter, prompting customers to bring shipments forward to the second quarter for fear of further price hikes, he said.

Shipments are expected to normalize this quarter, he said.

The company is considering raising prices further in the first quarter of next year if component costs remain high, Hwang said.

To address component shortages, Getac began increasing strategic inventory at the end of last year, Getac vice president of finance and accounting Vicky Hsieh (謝淑娟) said.

The company currently holds about three to four months’ worth of strategic inventory, with relatively little risk of write-downs, as the inventory can be gradually absorbed through normal operations, she added.

To meet rising demand for production capacity in Taiwan, the company would consider further expanding its Taoyuan plant, Hwang said.

Getac reported that net profit decreased 2.1 percent year-on-year to NT$1.29 billion during the third quarter. Earnings per share slid to NT$2.06 from NT$2.12 a year earlier.

Gross margin fell to 29.4 percent last quarter from 31.54 percent a year earlier, as some higher-margin rugged computer shipments were pulled forward into the second quarter, Hsieh said.

Gross margin is expected to recover to between 31.1 percent and 31.7 percent this quarter, supported by a more favorable product mix, she added.

data.title: US Congress eyes tighter curbs on chips to China
data.description:
US House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday there was growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China after a spy scandal forced out Nvidia Corp CEO Jensen Huang (黃仁勳), who has pushed to preserve access to the Chinese market and has close ties with US President Donald Trump.

Lawmakers from both parties have since called for tougher restrictions on China’s access to advanced artificial intelligence (AI) chips, threatening access to chips that underpin China’s surging AI development.

“The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here,” Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, told reporters at the US Capitol, adding he favored limiting China’s access to the advanced technology. “I think there’s a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take.”

The Chinese businesswoman at the center of the scandal, Alice Huang (黃樂), was an executive at Megaspeed, an Nvidia partner the US government suspects of helping China obtain advanced AI chips restricted under US export controls. Beijing has denied she is a spy.

Congressional Republicans are keen to attach new restrictions on exports of advanced AI chips to China to the annual defense authorization bill, a must-pass measure that authorizes military spending and typically attracts bipartisan support, according to a Senate aide, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

Lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four bills on chip exports, according to statements since Monday. The AI Overwatch Act would give Congress more power over advanced AI chip exports. The Chip Security Act would require companies to track the location of advanced AI processors to prevent smuggling.

The MATCH Act would pressure US allies to restrict sales and maintenance of advanced chipmaking equipment destined for China. The Remote Access Security Act would give the Commerce Department the tools to stop Chinese firms from renting overseas data centers to access Nvidia chips.

Jensen Huang’s resignation is unlikely to end congressional scrutiny of Nvidia and could leave the former chief executive more exposed to investigation, said Sunny Cheung, an analyst at the Washington-based Jamestown Foundation.

“Congress can still subpoena him and Nvidia should conduct an independent investigation to determine whether the problems extend beyond Huang,” Cheung said.

Cheung said Jensen Huang’s departure could weaken Nvidia’s influence in Washington and create additional momentum for legislation that tightens restrictions on advanced chip exports. He said Nvidia’s new leadership could also reconsider the company’s China strategy as it seeks to rebuild trust with US policymakers.

data.title: Hon Hai Q3 net income surged 34%
data.description:
PROMISING: The company expects demand to continue growing for its cloud and networking products, smart consumer electronics and computing products

Hon Hai Precision Industry Co (鴻海精密) yesterday reported record net profit in the third quarter, growing 34 percent year-on-year to NT$77.52 billion (US$2.36 billion), driven mainly by continued demand for artificial intelligence (AI) servers by major US cloud service providers.

“Even after the US midterm elections, we have not seen any slowdown in major cloud service providers’ [CSPs] spending plans, and we believe the short-term impact remains limited,” Hon Hai chairman Young Liu (劉揚偉) told an earnings conference in Taipei.

“However, we will continue to monitor whether there could be any longer-term impact,” he added.

Earnings per share rose to a record NT$5.51 from NT$4.15 a year earlier, beating analysts’ average estimate of NT$4.92.

Gross margin fell to 6.02 percent from 6.35 percent due to its product mix and higher key component costs, while operating margin rose to 3.83 percent from 3.43 percent on economies of scale and a lower expense ratio, Hon Hai chief financial officer David Huang (黃德財) said.

Full-year operating margin is expected to exceed last year’s 3.2 percent, he said.

Hon Hai is Apple Inc’s primary iPhone assembler and makes servers powered by Nvidia Corp’s AI accelerators.

The company expects AI server rack shipments to grow by a high double-digit percentage sequentially this quarter, with AI server revenue also rising quarter-on-quarter, Hon Hai spokesman James Wu (巫俊毅) said.

It further expects AI server rack shipments to grow by a high double-digit percentage next year from this year, Liu said.

The company has not seen any significant manufacturing challenges from the transition between old and new generations of server racks for its major US customer, as automation and vertical integration continue to improve production efficiency, he said.

Hon Hai has also been working with major CSPs on various application-specific integrated circuit (ASIC)-based AI servers, with shipments of ASIC-based models rising 150 percent year-on-year last quarter, he said.

Many of Hon Hai’s ASIC-based projects use a consignment model, under which chip costs are excluded from revenue, meaning their share of revenue could be lower than their share of shipments, he added.

This quarter, Hon Hai expects significant sequential growth in its cloud and networking products business, driven by the continued ramp-up of next-generation AI server racks, Liu said.

Revenue from smart consumer electronics is expected to grow robustly this quarter on peak-season smartphone demand and higher selling prices, while computing product revenue is expected to decline slightly due to memory supply constraints, he said.

Revenue from components and other products is also expected to grow significantly, he added.

Last quarter, cloud and networking products accounted for 54 percent of Hon Hai’s NT$3.02 trillion revenue, followed by smartphones at 29 percent, computing products at 12 percent and others at 5 percent, the company said.

Overall, Hon Hai remains optimistic about its performance this year and expects revenue to grow by a double-digit percentage next year, Liu said.

Capital expenditure totaled NT$161.72 billion in the first nine months, up 43 percent year-on-year, mainly for AI server capacity expansion across Hon Hai’s global manufacturing footprint, Huang said.

data.title: E Ink cuts sales growth forecast on slow demand
data.description:
E Ink Holdings Inc (元太科技), the world’s biggest e-paper display supplier, yesterday cuts its full-year revenue growth forecast for a second time to 9 percent, citing sluggish demand for consumer electronics including e-readers as surging memorychip costs drive up retail prices.

Despite the downgrade, the company still expects full-year revenue and profit to reach record highs, E Ink chairman Johnson Lee (李正昊) told an online earnings conference.

Three months ago, Lee projected revenue this year would expand at an annual rate of 10 to 15 percent from NT$36.12 billion (US$1.1 billion) last year.

“Unfortunately, we’ve fallen victim to the AI [artificial intelligence] boom,” Lee said. “Still, we remain fairly optimistic about our trajectory. Even without the AI hype, our business can continue to grow.”

Lee attributed the downgrade to a forecast 15 percent year-on-year drop in the consumer segment, but a projected 35 percent growth in the Internet of Things (IoT) business — driven by retail and electronic shelf labels (ESL) — should offset the decline.

Consequently, E Ink anticipates a structural shift in its revenue mix, as IoT sales are projected to surpass those of its consumer segment for the first time in its history, Lee said.

E Ink expects growth momentum to persist next year, fueled by robust demand for e-paper used in ESLs and digital signage, Lee said.

Growth would also be supported by improved yields on its new H5 production line, which manufactures wider films — a key material in e-paper production — resulting in a better cost structure, he said.

The company is also installing another line, H6, to produce even wider films than H5, he added.

Beyond its core e-paper display business, E Ink is expanding into polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) — commonly known as Teflon — through its 15.7 percent owned Taiflex Scientific Co (台虹), a leading Taiwanese supplier of flexible copper-clad laminates.

The potential shift to PTFE has become one of the hottest topics across the local printed circuit board supply chain, as Nvidia Corp looks to adopt the material for its next-generation servers.

E Ink plans to manufacture PTFE for Taiflex on a contract basis at its new factory in Taoyuan’s Guanyin District (觀音), Lee said.

The company expects PTFE production to generate a small amount of revenue next year before scaling up in 2028.

“Now that we are victims of AI in the consumer segment, we at least have to jump on the AI bandwagon through this,” Lee said.

E Ink reported NT$2.65 billion in net profit last quarter, slumping 37 percent year-on-year from NT$4.23 billion. The company attributed the decline to sagging demand for e-paper used in e-readers and e-notes. Gross margin dropped to 52.2 percent from 55.9 percent.

During the first three quarters, the company accumulated NT$9.17 billion in net profit, edging 2.45 percent lower from NT$9.4 billion in the same period last year.

Earnings per share slid to NT$7.94 from NT$8.17. Revenue dipped about 1 percent annually to NT$28.79 billion.

data.title: Taoyuan union ends talks with Micron after ‘defeat’
data.description:
A union representing workers at a Micron Technology Inc plant in Taiwan yesterday said that it would pull out of further talks with the US chip giant after “our defeat” in trying to secure a new profit-sharing deal.

Surging global demand for chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) data centers has sent revenues soaring for firms like Micron, and as their earnings skyrocket, workers are calling for a bigger cut of profits.

Micron, which makes about 50 to 60 percent of its memory chips in Taiwan, has been locked in weeks of talks over remuneration with a union representing hundreds of workers at its Taoyuan plant.

More than 2,000 employees had threatened to strike as they pushed for a bigger share of the company’s earnings. In the end, only a handful of employees stopped working for one day.

“We formally acknowledge that our campaign to secure a profit-sharing system has not been successful, and we must continue our efforts in the future,” the union representing the Taoyuan workers said in a statement, acknowledging “our defeat.”

The union said its members could go ahead with the company’s requirement to sign an agreement “waiving the right to future disputes” in order to receive “bonuses and other new employment benefits.”

It added it would “no longer participate” in negotiations on Tuesday next week.

Micron denied that it had required employees to “sign individual agreements or to waive any rights.”

“Micron respects team members’ lawful rights to organize a union and to engage in collective bargaining,” the company said in a statement, adding that it would “continue to seek constructive dialogue with the Taoyuan Union.”

At Micron’s larger plant in Taichung, the union representing thousands of workers there signed an agreement with the company last month after they “reached consensus on a number of matters,” a joint statement said at the time.

Micron had agreed to move to a quarterly profit-sharing bonus system, in addition to the annual bonus, and increase the company’s pension contribution, Micron Memory Taiwan Co (台灣美光) chairman Lu Donghui (盧東暉) said.

data.title: Taiwan weighting in three major indices raised: MSCI
data.description:
THIRD CONSECUTIVE INCREASE: Analysts attributed the upgrade to the tech-heavy Taiwan stock market’s strong showing on the back of the artificial intelligence boom

Global index provider MSCI Inc has raised Taiwan’s weighting in three of its major indices after a regular index review.

MSCI has upgraded Taiwan’s weighting in the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, the most closely watched by foreign institutional investors, from 28.86 percent to 29.01 percent, it said in a statement.

The index provider has also raised Taiwan’s weighting in the MSCI All-Country World Index from 3.25 percent to 3.28 percent and hiked the weighting in the MSCI All-Country Asia ex-Japan Index from 32.72 percent to 32.83 percent.

It was the third consecutive quarter in which MSCI has raised Taiwan’s weighting in the three indices simultaneously. Analysts attributed the upgrade to the recent strong showing by Taiwan’s tech-heavy stock market amid the global artificial intelligence (AI) boom.

In the MSCI Emerging Markets Index, India received the largest weighting upgrade of 0.17 percentage points, while China suffered the steepest downgrade of 0.13 percentage points, MSCI said.

In the MSCI Global Standard Indexes, it added three Taiwanese stocks: IC substrate maker Kinsus Interconnect Technology Corp (景碩), Nan Ya Printed Circuit Board Corp (南亞電路板) and copper-clad laminate supplier Taiwan Union Technology Corp (台燿).

The three stocks have been removed from the MSCI Global Small Cap Indexes.

MSCI had decided to add the three companies to the MSCI Global Standard Indexes in the August index review, but the trio’s soaring share prices led the Taiwan Stock Exchange to list them as “disposition stocks,” which faced trading restrictions, so the inclusion had been postponed until this month’s index review.

MSCI has deleted leasing and financial service provider Chailease Holding Co (中租控股), electronics paper supplier E Ink Holdings Inc (元太科技), connector producer Lotes Co (嘉澤) and container cargo shipper Wan Hai Lines Ltd (萬海航運) from the MSCI Global Standard Indexes, but added Chailease, E Ink and Lotes to the MSCI Global Small Cap Indexes.

MSCI has also added 15 Taiwanese stocks to the MSCI Global Small Cap Indexes, including server maker AIC Inc (營邦), motherboard supplier ASRock Industrial Computer Corp (東擎) and Web communication devices producer Browave Corp (波若威).

Nine additional Taiwanese stocks have been removed from the MSCI Global Small Cap Indexes, including fine carbon material provider China Steel Chemical Co (中碳), offshore maritime equipment supplier Dong Fang Offshore Co (東方風能), environmental protection solution provider ECOVE Environment Corp (崑鼎) and elevator manufacturer GFC Ltd (崇友).

After the index adjustments, Taiwan Union Technology enjoyed the largest weighting increase to 0.37 percent from zero in the MSCI Taiwan Index, while Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co (台積電) saw its weighting cut by 0.25 percentage points, the steepest decrease, to 54.29 percent.

The latest index adjustments are set to take effect after the market closes on Nov. 30.

MSCI index reviews are conducted in February, May, August and November each year. The indexes, provided in US dollar terms, help guide professional investors in adjusting their portfolios.
